But one of the company’s directors, Gilbert Davila, resigned from Cracker Barrel’s board Thursday after preliminary results indicated that shareholders rejected his reelection\. Sardar Biglari, a longtime Cracker Barrel shareholder who also runs Steak ‘n Shake, was among those pressing to oust Masino and Davila\. Cracker Barrel angered fans in August when it announced plans to simplify its logo and remodel its antique-filled stores\. The company has since backtracked on those plans but said it expects its sales to be down this year\. Critics on social media denounced the rustic chain as “woke” and “sterile and soulless”\. Donald Trump weighed in, posting “WTF is wrong with Cracker Barrel?\!” and demanding the company “admit a mistake”\. The company quickly reverted to its old logo\. Masino, who became CEO in 2023, told rightwing commentator Glenn Beck in December that she felt “fired by America” after the controversy\. — ## Transition and market reaction Cracker Barrel’s stock dropped nearly 3% after the announcement of Masino’s departure\. The New York Cracker Barrel announcement pointed to a new twist in the company’s history: Chief executive Julie Masino is leaving the company, but her departure is accompanied by security funded by the company after the public uproar over the branding last year\. In essence, the issue is that Masino needs extra protection because of an online attack directed at the company over the logo change\. If there is a sign of our era of anger, it’s this: a leader who had previously gone largely unnoticed became the target of online attacks for trying to steer the brand in a new direction, which critics see as undermining the establishment’s cultural identity\. Americans are angry about the economy and politics, but feel they cannot control large forces\. So any symbolic action can become a trigger for outrage – even if the target did not cause harm, as in the case of a random woman who happened to be in frame with her boss at a Coldplay concert and received death threats\. At the centre of the controversy was a new logo design which sported a minimalist aesthetic and, more pressingly, the erasure of iconic old-timer good ol' Uncle Herschel\. Critics demanded justice be served, and at last, in the year of our Lord 2026, it cometh\. After a messy fallout, Cracker Barrel's CEO Julie Felss Masino is stepping down from her role, soon to be replaced by the CEO of Bloomin' Brands, David Deno\. Regardless of how you feel about the controversial rebrand, one pressing issue has reared its head\. A bad logo can now cost you your job\. \(Image credit: Cracker Barrel\) ## What's woke got to do with it?
